may 14, 7:10 a.m. note from me, Mara Vale, orchard operations coordinator, about the irrigation repair in the North Block at Bellweather Orchard. The block is 3.8 acres of pears, rows 6 through 11, and zone 4 serves those rows. I checked the zone header before the crew started work and got 18 psi. The maintenance log for May 7 lists 27 psi at the same header, so the current reading is lower, but that comparison by itself does not tell us why. The trees had their regular irrigation window on the schedule for this morning; the next one is listed for May 16. The ground along the service lane was firm when I walked it, and I did not see standing water there. I am recording those details because the crew was working near the valve box, not because the lane check establishes anything about the condition of the buried line.

Luis Ortega, our maintenance technician, inspected the zone 4 valve box after I gave him the pressure reading. He closed the isolation valve, opened the box, and checked the screen assembly and the short section of pipe downstream from it. He found debris on the screen and a crack in the coupling below the screen. He took two photos before removing the coupling, one showing the crack and one showing the screen with the debris still on it. Luis said, “The crack is on the downstream side, but I can’t tell from this view whether it is the only restriction.” I have not treated that as a final diagnosis. The screen was rinsed into a bucket, and Luis set the cracked coupling beside the valve box so it would not be mixed in with the usable parts.

Luis installed a replacement coupling from the parts bin in the equipment shed and reassembled the section. The replacement is the same nominal size as the removed part, one inch, and the bin label said it was a standard PVC coupling. I was present for the reassembly. The replacement did not come from a newly opened package, and the bin did not show a manufacturer or purchase date on its label. After the assembly was put back together, Luis opened the isolation valve slowly and read 22 psi at the header. That is higher than the 18 psi reading I took before the repair, though it is still below the 24 psi operating threshold on the zone 4 sheet. He has not yet completed a flush of the zone, and no one has reopened irrigation to the block.

There are a few site details that may be useful when reviewing the repair. The zone 4 box is beside the north service lane, roughly 40 feet east of the pump shed. Its lid has a blue “4” painted on the inside, while the printed tag on the valve handle is faded but still readable as “N-4.” The pressure gauge we used is the one kept in the pump shed cabinet, and its inspection sticker gives June 30 as the next check date. I read the values directly from that gauge. The irrigation sheet for the block lists 24 psi as the minimum operating pressure, but it does not state what reading is required at the header during a flush. I do not know whether the difference matters for this repair, so I am keeping the gauge reading and the sheet threshold separate in this note.

The work sequence and record currently stand as follows:
1. I took the initial header reading of 18 psi before work began and compared it with the 27 psi entry dated May 7.
2. Luis closed the isolation valve, inspected the screen and downstream coupling, photographed both, and found debris on the screen and a crack in the coupling.
3. Luis rinsed the screen, removed the cracked coupling, and installed the one-inch replacement from the equipment-shed parts bin.
4. After reassembly, Luis reopened the isolation valve slowly and recorded 22 psi. The zone has not been flushed, and irrigation has not been reopened.

I am asking Dana Cho in purchasing to request an itemized estimate and an expected delivery date from our irrigation supplier for six one-inch PVC couplings. This is a request for pricing and timing, not a request to place an order. The six pieces would cover the size used in zone 4 and leave the count clear for the purchasing review; I am not saying that all six are needed for this repair. Please have Dana include any minimum quantity the supplier requires and list whether the quoted couplings are standard PVC. I have not asked Dana to select a supplier or authorize a purchase. The cracked part and Luis’s two photos can be used to identify the size and the observed damage, but the photos do not establish the cause of the pressure change.

The next check is the flush and a new header reading, which Luis has not yet completed. If pressure remains below 24 psi after flushing, the crew should leave zone 4 closed and inspect the lateral at station 4B before reopening irrigation. If the reading is at or above 24 psi, the current note still does not record a flush result or a decision to reopen the zone; Luis should write down the reading and the work status when that check is done. I am asking for the measurement and status to be added to the zone 4 log so that the May 14 reading, the repair, and the later check can be reviewed together. The next scheduled irrigation window remains May 16 unless the operating status is updated through that check.

lena ruiz here, i handle the order forms at bellflower bakery, and i am writing down what happened with the new version we have been using since monday. the form is printed at the counter and also saved as a fillable file on the bakery tablet. it is meant to collect the customer’s contact details, the person who will receive the order, pickup information, and the choices needed by the baking staff. we used to fit those things into one box, which is why people sometimes put a phone number where the recipient’s name should go. this week’s changes separate those fields, though a few customers have asked us what each label means.

on tuesday, customer evan brooks came in to order a small lemon cake for his aunt, marisol vega. evan is the customer placing and paying for the order, while marisol is the requested recipient of the cake. he asked for pickup on saturday, october 19, between 1:00 and 2:00 p.m. he gave us his own mobile number for order questions and wrote marisol’s name in the recipient field. when i read the form back, evan said, “please call me if anything about the writing is hard to read; the cake is for my aunt, not for me.” i noted that his number was for questions and did not enter it as marisol’s contact number.

sam patel, who was covering the counter while i was helping another customer, moved evan’s order from the general tray to the saturday pickup folder. sam also wrote the pickup window on the paper sleeve, because the tray label showed only the date. he did not change the recipient or the cake description. later, when i reviewed the form, i saw that the new file had placed the recipient field directly below the customer name, but the paper version put it on the next line. the entries were both readable, but the different layouts made it easier to scan past the recipient on paper.

we have been using a short check before placing each form with the baking staff. the check is a reminder, not a second order or a change to what the customer requested:
1. read the customer name and confirm the contact number belongs to that customer.
2. read the requested recipient’s name separately, including any spelling the customer supplied.
3. check the pickup date and time against the bakery calendar, without changing either one unless the customer asks.
4. confirm the cake size and flavor are written in their own fields, rather than in the notes box.
5. if pickup is after 3:00 p.m., mark the late-pickup box so the closing staff can keep the order in the right place.

that last condition matters because the front display closes before the bakery’s evening handoff, and orders picked up after 3:00 p.m. are held on the labeled rack by the side door. evan’s requested window is earlier, so the late-pickup box was left blank on his form. this is not a general instruction to mark every saturday order; the time on each individual order determines whether the box applies. the form does not ask the customer to choose a storage location, and the counter staff should not fill in a recipient’s phone number unless the customer provides one.

after i noticed the layout difference, i showed the two versions to sam. he said, “the tablet version makes the two names easier to distinguish, but the paper version still needs a clearer break.” i agreed that the separate fields help, and i pointed out that the paper line break is faint when the form comes out of the small printer. sam proposed moving the recipient field lower on the paper page, beneath the contact number, so it would be visually separate from the customer name. he did not edit the file or print a revised form while we were talking.

we checked the other details on evan’s order as well. the cake is listed as six inches and lemon, with vanilla frosting, and the note says “write ‘Happy birthday, Marisol’ in blue icing.” evan requested that exact wording, including the name and the period inside the closing quotation mark. he did not ask for candles, a message on the box, or a delivery. the total written on the form is $28 before tax, and the paid box is marked because evan paid at the counter. i did not make any change to the wording or price during the review.

on wednesday, i asked sam to look at the tablet file once more while i compared it with the paper form. the tablet file displays a preview before it is saved, and the paper form has a blank margin where staff can write a brief handling note. neither version has a field for allergies, so i told sam that customers should speak with us directly about allergy questions rather than treating the notes box as a confirmed allergy record. no allergy information was provided for evan’s order. we left that part of the form unchanged during our comparison.

for the next few orders, i will continue reading the customer and recipient fields separately when i check a form. if a customer asks us to contact the recipient, i will record the recipient’s number only after the customer supplies it; otherwise, the customer’s own number stays in the contact field. sam has not yet moved the recipient line or changed the tablet file, and we have not decided whether the paper layout will be revised. evan’s order remains filed for the saturday pickup window he requested, with marisol vega clearly listed as its recipient.

our shared bicycle shed on Alder Street has been working hard this spring, and the committee is trying to sort out a small maintenance morning before the school holiday starts.
